opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what that project meant to me personally, more than how it performed by any external metric.

HED was really my first serious piece of research. I did it during my PhD at UC San Diego with my advisor, Zhuowen Tu, back around 2015. That was a very particular moment. Deep learning had just started to take over computer vision, and most people were applying convolutional networks to image classification. Edge detection felt like an old, classic problem, something people had worked on for decades with hand-designed filters and carefully engineered features.

What excited me was the idea that you could approach this low-level task end to end, from image to image, with a deep network, and that you could use the network's internal hierarchy in a meaningful way. The "holistically-nested" part was about taking side outputs from different layers, supervising them directly, and fusing them. Shallow layers capture fine local detail, deeper layers capture more semantic, global structure, and you let the model learn how to combine them. Looking back, a lot of that thinking, such as deep supervision, multi-scale feature fusion, and dense prediction with fully convolutional networks, became pretty standard later. At the time it felt like we were figuring it out from scratch.

So my pride isn't really about the number. Citations reflect how many people work in a particular area, and edge detection is a relatively niche topic compared with backbone architectures or generative models. A paper like ResNeXt naturally gets cited much more because everyone uses backbones. But in terms of the experience of doing research, HED was where I first learned what it feels like to have an idea, struggle with it, see it actually work, and realize it says something a bit more general about how these networks represent the visual world.

It also shaped my taste. It taught me that a good piece of work doesn't need to chase the hottest benchmark. It can take a problem people think is "solved" or old-fashioned and look at it through a new lens. I still care about that kind of work, where the idea is clean and you really understand why it works. To me, that matters more than whether it becomes the most-cited paper on my list.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the citations to edge detection being a niche topic and contrasts it with widely used backbones; it does not say HED received fewer citations because it solved its problem.

r002.rationale: It describes HED’s side outputs, deep supervision, and fusion for edge detection, but does not characterize it as applying Deeply Supervised Nets to a pixel-labeling task.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, HED is the work I'm most emotionally attached to, even though it's nowhere near my most cited paper. It was my first first-author project in the deep learning era, done with my advisor Zhuowen Tu at UCSD around 2014, 2015. At that time, edge detection was considered a kind of solved, boring, old-fashioned problem. Everyone was rushing to classification, to detection, to the big ImageNet-style tasks. Edge detection felt like something from the Canny era that people had moved past.

But I thought it was a beautiful problem precisely because it's so primitive. Edges sit at the boundary between low-level vision and high-level understanding. To know where an object boundary is, you actually need to know something about what the object is. So the question I was asking was, can a network learn this end to end, from pixels to edges, with multi-scale information fused inside the network rather than hand-engineered outside it. The side outputs, the deep supervision at multiple scales, the holistic image-to-image prediction, those ideas felt very natural to me and they turned out to generalize well beyond edges.

The reason I'm proud of it has less to do with the result and more with the mindset. It taught me to pick problems because I find them genuinely interesting, not because they're fashionable. It also taught me that a clean idea on a small, well-defined problem can quietly influence a lot of later work, even if the citation counter doesn't show it. People working on segmentation, on dense prediction, on multi-scale feature fusion, many of them absorbed those ideas without necessarily citing a paper about edges.

And personally, it was where I learned how to do research: how to form a hypothesis, how to design an experiment that actually tests it, how to write. Citations measure impact, but they don't measure what a piece of work did to you as a researcher. HED shaped how I think, and that's why it still matters to me.

r002.rationale: It describes HED’s pixel-to-edge, image-to-image prediction using side outputs and deep supervision at multiple scales, which conveys deeply supervised networks applied to a pixel-labeling task.

For me, the deeper question is whether the work brought clarity to a problem—whether it offered a simple, coherent way to think about it. That’s what makes Holistic Edge Detection meaningful to me. A paper can have fewer citations and still represent the kind of research you really value.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m proud of it because it captured a way of thinking about research that still matters to me: take a fundamental problem and find a simple, coherent way to approach it. With Holistically-Nested Edge Detection, we brought information from different levels of a network together and trained them jointly for edge detection. It was a very satisfying connection between the architecture and the problem.

Citations are one signal of impact, but they’re not the whole story. For me, the pride comes from the idea, how clearly it worked, and how much I learned through developing it.
